source.title: Athletic groin pain (part 2): a prospective cohort study on the biomechanical evaluation of change of direction identifies three clusters of movement patterns

paper.citation: Franklyn-Miller, A., Richter, C., King, E., Gore, S., Moran, K., Strike, S., & Falvey, E. C. (2017). Athletic groin pain (part 2): A prospective cohort study on the biomechanical evaluation of change of direction identifies three clusters of movement patterns. British Journal of Sports Medicine, 51(5), 460–468. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2016-096050
paper.abstract: Can athletes with chronic athletic groin pain be grouped by distinct three-dimensional movement strategies during a maximal planned cut, and are those strategies associated with clinical anatomical diagnoses? Analysis included 322 symptomatic athletes, mean age 27.6 years, with a median 36 weeks (IQR 16–75) from symptom onset to presentation. Participants came from the same chronic athletic-groin-pain referral cohort described in the companion diagnostic study. Thirty-one of 382 eligible participants missed motion analysis and 29 were excluded for partial or double force-platform contacts. Prospective cohort biomechanical analysis of three maximal-effort trials per direction during a planned 110° cutting manoeuvre after a standardized warm-up and practice trials. Eight-camera motion capture and two force platforms recorded whole-body kinematics and ground-reaction forces; inverse dynamics produced tri-planar joint moments and work estimates. Hierarchical clustering used phase-based waveform scores from ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, and thorax kinematics and ankle, knee, and hip kinetics; gap statistics selected a three-cluster solution. Statistical parametric mapping and pointwise Cohen's d characterized waveform differences, and chi-square testing evaluated cluster–diagnosis relationships.
paper.tldr: This study examines whole-body change-of-direction strategies in athletes with chronic groin pain and tests whether movement clusters map onto anatomical diagnoses. Three movement-strategy clusters contained 128 (40%), 62 (19%), and 132 (41%) athletes. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort biomechanical analysis of three maximal-effort trials per direction during a planned 110° cutting manoeuvre after a standardized warm-up and practice trials. Eight-camera motion capture and two force platforms recorded whole-body kinematics and ground-reaction forces; inverse dynamics produced tri-planar joint moments and work estimates. Hierarchical clustering used phase-based waveform scores from ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, and thorax kinematics and ankle, knee, and hip kinetics; gap statistics selected a three-cluster solution. Statistical parametric mapping and pointwise Cohen's d characterized waveform differences, and chi-square testing evaluated cluster–diagnosis relationships.
paper.findings: Three movement-strategy clusters contained 128 (40%), 62 (19%), and 132 (41%) athletes. The clusters differed across ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, thorax, ground-contact time, and joint-work patterns; for example, cluster 3 showed less hip and knee flexion, more contralateral pelvic drop, and predominantly ankle work relative to the other clusters. Anatomical diagnoses did not differ significantly across movement clusters (p>0.644); pubic-aponeurosis diagnoses were distributed similarly across clusters. The observed strategies therefore described heterogeneous load-distribution patterns within a symptomatic cohort but did not identify a movement signature for a particular pain location or anatomical diagnosis.
paper.limitations: The study had no uninjured comparison group, so it cannot determine whether any cluster represents abnormal, causal, protective, or compensatory movement. The authors explicitly state that the optimal movement pattern remains unknown. Cluster selection depended on the symptomatic or MRI-confirmed side, with random side selection when both sides were affected; this simplifies bilateral presentations. The planned laboratory cut and cohort-specific clustering do not establish prospective injury risk or individualized rehabilitation efficacy. Movement–diagnosis independence argues against assigning a rehabilitation target solely from an anatomical label or cluster membership.
paper.practicalImplications: Three-dimensional analysis may broaden assessment beyond the painful structure, but these clusters are descriptive rather than prescriptive. Use movement analysis to generate athlete-specific hypotheses about load distribution and to monitor task performance; do not treat a cluster as a diagnosis, injury-risk category, or validated rehabilitation template.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. Use movement analysis to generate athlete-specific hypotheses about load distribution and to monitor task performance; do not treat a cluster as a diagnosis, injury-risk category, or validated rehabilitation template. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, three-dimensional analysis may broaden assessment beyond the painful structure, but these clusters are descriptive rather than prescriptive. Use movement analysis to generate athlete-specific hypotheses about load distribution and to monitor task performance; do not treat a cluster as a diagnosis, injury-risk category, or validated rehabilitation template. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
